## Voice of the age: ideas for later

- **The scribe.** Tushratta spoke Hurrian, his scribe wrote Akkadian, and an Egyptian scribe read it out to Pharaoh; Finkel imagines a scribe softening an angry letter on the way. In the game the scribe does not relay or alter messages, unless he is in someone else's pay ("A king seals what his scribe wrote"): otherwise he has no motive to, and one mediator keeps the trail readable (see "Languages"). His role is what he knows. He writes his king's tablets and reads the foreign ones, so he holds the court's secrets: bribable, spyable, a source of leaks (see "What servants know").
- **Envoy rank.** A high-standing envoy is more credible and costs more; a nobody is cheap and easily dismissed. A public fact or calling could carry it.
- **The chancery archive.** Egyptian clerks noted on incoming letters what had been promised and sent, to settle later disputes. It is the period form of the per-court ledger of promises in the risk table.
- **Failure at home.** Rib-Hadda's brother drove him out of Byblos after his messenger came back from Egypt empty-handed. Standing at home depends on what one's letters bring back; a natural rule for speaking city-states (question 12).
- **The queen mother as a channel.** Writing to someone at a king's court other than the king, a cheap form of the resident envoy (question 14).
